# The exact-kernel MeshTransformer on industrial data: AirFRANS and DrivAerML {#sec-industrial-mt1}

On solver-labelled industrial data the exact-kernel MeshTransformer (MT1
after this point) is an accurate but narrow regressor. On AirFRANS, a 2D
RANS airfoil benchmark, it matches the AirFRANS-paper baselines on
velocity and is about 10x behind MARIO and 70x behind GLOBE in the same
table; on surface pressure it is about 4x better than MARIO and about 18x
behind GLOBE; and its recommended configuration extrapolates to unseen
Reynolds numbers and angles of attack within 1.2–2x of its
in-distribution error. On
DrivAerML, a 3D vehicle benchmark, its gain over the plain architecture
comes almost entirely from the boundary-trace formulation (3.8x at the
operating configuration) and from capacity (2.4x); the exact singular
kernels that motivate the architecture contribute 0–8%. Every tested
checkpoint diverges when evaluated zero-shot on a different vehicle
family, and every checkpoint's accuracy is specific to the surface
sampling density it was trained at. The exact-kernel line's measured
strengths on industrial data are parameter efficiency and the exact
contracts it carries, not accuracy or transfer.

The controlled suites (@sec-linear-suites) establish what exact operator
structure buys when the labels are exact and the PDE is linear. The two
datasets here add what those suites cannot: labels from a turbulence
closure that no exact kernel describes, Reynolds-number variation across
cases, and real geometry with real meshing. The datasets and splits are
defined in @sec-datasets; the metric conventions in @sec-metrics; the
fair-comparison protocol in @sec-fair-comparison.

## AirFRANS {#sec-airfrans}

AirFRANS is 1,000 steady incompressible RANS solutions (OpenFOAM,
eddy-viscosity closure) over NACA airfoils at Reynolds numbers of 2–6
million and angles of attack from −5° to +15°, with velocity, pressure
and turbulent viscosity at roughly 180,000 mesh points per case. It maps
onto the boundary-to-field problem of @sec-problem directly: the airfoil
boundary carries a no-slip label and geometry only, the freestream enters
as a global unit drive direction, and the Reynolds number enters as one
dimensionless global scalar, ln Re. The model predicts the disturbance
velocity ΔU = U − U∞ normalised by |U∞| (the freestream is the exact
solution at infinity, so it is added back rather than learned), the
pressure coefficient C_p, and ln(1 + ν_t/ν) at interior query points.
Two contracts from the exact-label suites are deliberately not declared:
drive linearity (RANS is nonlinear) and monopole-free deflation (a
lifting airfoil carries net circulation, which that contract removes).

The task is the official `scarce` split: 200 training cases and 200 test
cases. Validation for checkpoint selection is 8 cases carved from the
training cases by a fixed protocol seed (192 cases train), and the
official test set is scored once per checkpoint. Training uses the full
airfoil boundary every step and 4,096 volume query points per iteration
(GLOBE's sampling), a Huber loss, and a cosine learning-rate schedule
from 1.41 × 10⁻³ to 1/64 of that value; 3–5 seeds per configuration.
Cases with energy-conservation violations (C_pt > 1.02, 0.003% of points)
are excluded identically from training and evaluation of every arm.

The metric is the benchmark's own: per-sample z-score mean squared
error. For each test case and field, the squared error is divided by the
variance of that case's true field and averaged over its points; the
result is averaged over cases. A mean predictor scores 1.0. Lower is
better, and all published AirFRANS numbers are in this unit. Where the
text says "pooled convention" the normalisation is instead the pooled
training-set variance of the physical field; within-program ratios are
the same in both conventions to within seed spread, but absolute values
are not, and the two are never mixed in one table.

### Results {#sec-airfrans-results}

Five mechanisms, each tested as a single-factor change against the
reference configuration (one encoder layer, one head, two exact singular
kernel members, nonlinear field mode), account for the whole accuracy
ladder, and the largest rung is a feature change with zero new
parameters. The table gives each mechanism's effect on the x-velocity
z-score MSE at 3–5 seeds; the effect column is the ratio of the error
without the mechanism to the error with it (greater than 1 means the
mechanism helps).

| mechanism | what it adds | effect on u_x error |
|---|---|---|
| cosine schedule to GLOBE's endpoints | replaces a flat learning rate | 1.13x |
| 2D pseudoscalar (parity-odd) channel | a handed sector for lift and circulation | ~1.15x at reference capacity; no gain once log-radial features are present |
| far-field decay envelope (r⁻² on the direct drive) | the exterior-domain structure that closes the exact-label far-field ladder | 0.8x (worse) |
| eight learned smooth kernel members | a learned pair-radial pathway beside the two exact members | 6x |
| log-radial pair features (ln(a+ε), b/√(a+ε), v·r/√(a+ε)) fed to the learned members | power-law radial scales made linearly learnable | 1.66x |

: The AirFRANS mechanism ladder. Each row is a single-factor change on
the scarce split at 3–5 seeds; the effect is the ratio of x-velocity
z-score MSE without to with the mechanism. Not reproducible from
`results/`; transcribed from `output/airfrans_sweep` run logs (notebook
record @sec-nb-airfrans-v1, @sec-nb-h4-verdict). {#tbl-airfrans-ladder}

Two rows carry lessons beyond this dataset. The decay envelope is
exactly enforced and exactly wrong: a wake does not decay like a point
singularity, so a contract that is correct for exterior Laplace problems
costs 20% here. The learned-member rung is a parsimony result: a variant
that declares the viscous scale (Re^{−1/2} times the gauge, entering the
pair kernels as additional r/δ-normalised invariants) loses by about 6x
to identical members without the declaration. The reference decoder has
no learned dependence on pair distance at all (its only radial structure
is the two exact members), so the deficit is a missing pathway, not a
missing physical constant.

**The head-to-head on the scarce split.** The recommended configuration
(learned members with log-radial features) at three seeds, official test
set scored once, against the published single-run values. GLOBE has
117k parameters; the recommended arm has ≈202k; the other published
models are larger. Training budgets are matched to GLOBE's sampling
(4,096 queries per iteration) but not audited against the published
models' schedules, so this is a comparison against published tables,
not a resource-matched one.

| field | best dataset baseline | Transolver | MARIO | GLOBE | MT1, members + log-radial |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| u_x | 0.0146 | 0.0211 | 0.0015 | 0.00021 | 0.0145–0.0159 |
| C_p on the surface | 0.147 | 0.2367 | 0.027 | 0.00039 | ≈0.007 |

: Per-sample z-score MSE on the official AirFRANS scarce test set.
Published columns are single reported values; the MT1 column is the
range over three seeds. Not reproducible from `results/`; the MT1 column
is transcribed from `output/airfrans_sweep` re-score logs.
{#tbl-airfrans-headtohead}

On velocity MT1 matches the AirFRANS-paper baselines (its three-seed
range brackets GraphSAGE's 0.0146, the best of the four) and is about 10x
behind MARIO and 70x behind GLOBE in the same table; on surface pressure
it is about 4x better than MARIO and about 18x behind GLOBE. The gap to
GLOBE is the measure of what GLOBE's bespoke components (hyperlayers,
Padé kernels, multi-scale expansion) buy over the transformer-native
simplification on this problem. The parity-odd channel is not in the recommended
configuration: at three seeds its surface pressure sits at
mean-predictor level (z-score MSE 1.0–1.5) even though its velocity is
competitive, and its velocity gain disappears once the log-radial
features are present (composed, 0.0135–0.0155 pooled at three seeds
against 0.0128 for the features alone): both supply the same missing
power-law radial structure, and the feature carrier is cheaper.

**Learned log-radial scales are the largest single rung.** The
log-radial features add no parameters and declare nothing; they change
the arguments of the learned members so that a power law in pair
distance is a linear function of the inputs. Pooled convention, test
split, seeds free of the tail anomaly described below: members alone
0.0213 (5/5 seeds), members with log-radial features 0.0128 (4/5), a
1.66x gain. This is the same conclusion as the viscous-scale result by a
different route: the boundary-layer scale the declaration tries to
inject is better learned.

**Reynolds and angle-of-attack extrapolation.** The official
`reynolds` and `aoa` extrapolation tasks hold out Reynolds numbers and
angles of attack outside the training range. Evaluated zero-shot from
scarce-trained checkpoints (no fine-tuning), per-sample convention,
x-velocity z-score MSE:

| configuration | Re extrapolation | AoA extrapolation | in-distribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| two exact members only | 0.118–0.122 | 0.119–0.123 | — |
| members + log-radial features | 0.0147–0.0190 | 0.0208–0.0268 | 0.0128 (pooled) |
| members, doubled width (1.13M parameters) | 0.0159–0.0224 (4/5 seeds) | 0.0212–0.0297 | — |

: Zero-shot extrapolation on the official held-out AirFRANS splits;
ranges over seeds. The fifth wide seed reaches 0.101 on the Reynolds
split while clean in-distribution, the tail anomaly below surfacing under
extrapolation stress. Not reproducible from `results/`; transcribed from
`output/airfrans_evalx` run logs. {#tbl-airfrans-extrap}

The recommended configuration extrapolates to within roughly 1.2–2x of
its own in-distribution error on both axes, where the two-member
reference configuration degrades about 10x. Scope: the extrapolation
checkpoints were selected under a validation partition drawn from the
scarce test cases, which the extrapolation splits do not contain; the
in-distribution column is the clean-partition value.

**The surface task.** A companion task with the airfoil panel centroids
as queries tests whether the boundary-trace formulation that dominates
the DrivAerML result (@sec-drivaerml-trace-factorial) also helps in 2D.
It helps weakly: the trace arm wins on 4 of 5 seeds under both metric
conventions, by 1.2–1.35x in the median, inside the arm's own seed
spread. Consistent with DrivAerML, the trace defect is a learnable but
slow bias, absorbed where the budget allows (2D, 1,000 epochs) and worth
several-fold where it does not (3D, 500 epochs). The trace mode is exact
and free, so it stays on.

**The tail anomaly is learning-rate gated, deterministic and partly
essential.** Across the learned-member configurations at the protocol
learning rate, a minority of seeds diverge in a single velocity field
while the other fields stay clean. The census: members 0/5, members with
log-radial features 1/5, 16 members 1/3, 32 members 1/3, doubled width
0/5, learning rate halved 1/5, quartered 0/5. Three measured properties
pin it down. It is deterministic given the seed: an exact replication
reproduces an anomalous seed's divergence to four significant digits.
It is learning-rate gated: the log-radial configuration at 0.71x the
protocol rate shows 0/5 anomalies; the seed that scores 0.100 at the
protocol rate scores 0.0156 at the reduced rate. And the edge is partly
where the accuracy lives:
the backoff costs 22% in the clean-seed median (0.0156 against 0.0128).
The practical consequence is to run learned-member configurations at the
protocol rate with at least five seeds and report the census, since the
anomalies are single-field, detectable and seed-pinned.

## DrivAerML {#sec-drivaerml}

DrivAerML is 484 parametrically morphed DrivAer notchback variants with
time-averaged surface pressure and wall shear from scale-resolving CFD on
vehicle surfaces of roughly 8.8 million cells each (@sec-datasets). The
curated variant used here carries the posed boundary-value problem: five
typed boundary meshes (vehicle, no-slip ground plane, slip tunnel walls
and ceiling, inlet, outlet) and per-case freestream values. MT1 consumes
typed boundaries natively, but feeding all five boundaries does not help
on the surface task: vehicle-only 0.1019, all five 0.1026, per-boundary
pooled 0.1036 (one seed each, matched protocol, in the validation unit
defined next). At 722 panels for an entire ground plane the far
boundaries carry no exploitable signal beyond the freestream vector, so
every result below uses the vehicle surface only, the same information
diet as GeoTransolver.

The split is 435 training and 48 validation cars. Every case is
represented by 10,000 surface cells sampled from the vehicle mesh; the
same cells are the sources and the queries (the trace formulation
declares the query mesh to be the boundary). Training is 500 epochs, one
node (108 optimizer steps per epoch) unless stated, and the model
predicts surface pressure and the wall-shear vector at the sampled
cells.

**The validation unit.** The training recipe's validation metric is
target-normalised relative mean squared error: for each case and field,
Σ(ŷ − y)² / Σy² with area weights over the 10,000 cells, averaged over
the two fields and the 48 cars. It is the *square* of the relative L2
error used elsewhere in this book (@sec-metrics), so a ratio of 4x in
this unit is 2x in relative L2. Every number in the ladder, the
factorials and the frontier below is in this unit; the evaluation-harness
numbers in the generalization sections are relative L2 and are labelled
as such.

### Results {#sec-drivaerml-results}

Seven named steps take the reference MT1 from 0.1019 to 0.0058 in the
validation unit; one of them is protocol rather than architecture, and
the endpoint sits 2.34x above the matched GeoTransolver control at
matched parameter count. Each step is a single change on the
configuration to its left.

| step | change | validation rel. MSE | factor |
|---|---|---|---|
| reference | one encoder layer, two exact members, 16-GPU protocol | 0.1019 | — |
| trace | exterior-trace formulation (jump correction + own-cell readouts) | 0.0503 | 2.03x |
| batch | same configuration, one node (108 vs 27 steps/epoch) | 0.0288 | 1.75x |
| depth | two encoder layers (3 seeds: 0.0228/0.0224/0.0212) | 0.0224 | 1.29x |
| composition | + eight learned members + doubled width (3 seeds: 0.0138/0.0140/0.0156) | 0.0140 | 1.60x |
| scale, width | channel dimensions ×2 (4 runs: 0.0090–0.0114) | 0.0098 | 1.43x |
| scale, depth | + four encoder layers | 0.00702 | 1.40x |
| scale, depth | + eight encoder layers | 0.005828 | 1.20x |

: The DrivAerML ladder in the validation unit (relative MSE; relative L2
is the square root). "Composition" is the flagship configuration used
for every factorial below (≈0.8M parameters). Not reproducible from
`results/`; transcribed from `output/drivaer_t2` and `output/drivaer_hc2`
run logs. {#tbl-drivaerml-ladder}

The batch step is an optimisation effect, not an architectural one, and
it does not transfer to GeoTransolver, which finishes within 2% of itself
at one node and at 16 GPUs. A 16-GPU run for 2,000 epochs, matching the
one-node run's optimizer-update count, finishes at 0.0212 against 0.0221
for 500 epochs and 0.0140 at one node: quadrupling the updates recovers
about 11% of the small-batch advantage, so the effect is gradient noise,
not step count. The penalty holds at every scale (1.56–2.2x for
four-node against one-node twins), which is why every rung is trained on
one node.

Within the capacity ladder, depth is selective and rank is not: doubling
the attention rank changes nothing (0.0284 against 0.0288), doubling the
encoder depth gains 26%, and exchange rounds at matched parameters give
nothing (4 rounds 0.0146, 8 rounds 0.0198 against 0.0140). Pure width
bends under a learning-rate constraint: the ×4-width rung freezes at
initialisation at the shared learning rate in both seeds and, trained at
a quarter of it, finishes at 0.0123, worse than ×2 width with four times
the parameters. The frontier below therefore runs along the mixed
width-and-depth direction.

**The matched GeoTransolver control and where the gap lives.**
GeoTransolver (9.0M parameters, 12 layers, hidden 256, 256 slices;
@sec-baselines) trained on the identical trainer, split, sampling,
epochs and one-node protocol finishes at 0.00249. Against the flagship
that is 5.6x in relative MSE (2.4x in relative L2); against the
largest rung, 11.4M parameters by count, 2.34x (1.53x in relative L2).
Resources are not matched: GeoTransolver trains in 4.6 GB peak memory
and about 3.6 hours (500 epochs, four GB300 GPUs, 10,000 cells), the
0.8M-parameter flagship needs 35.8 GB and about 12.8 hours, and the
11.4M rung 104 GB (55.8 GB with checkpointed decode) and about 14
hours. The kernel decoder's dense pairwise evaluation is where the
memory goes (@sec-scale-ckpt); the extra memory buys MT1 no accuracy,
since the same function evaluated chunk-wise gives the same result.
GeoTransolver also reaches any given error about 25x earlier in epochs
on this trainer; local-geometry shortcuts are excluded as the reason,
because adding local geometric information to the decoder, restricting it
to a subtended-angle near field, or replacing it with a matched-width
global latent moves neither the efficiency curve nor the floor on the
deep configuration (0.0213 against 0.0225–0.0227 at epoch 300, one seed).

### The trace formulation carries the gain {#sec-drivaerml-trace-factorial}

Surface queries sit exactly on the double-layer kernel's jump
discontinuity. Evaluated naively, the closed form returns the interior
limit (−½ times the density) where the physics needs the exterior trace
(+½). Declaring the query mesh to be the boundary licenses two things: an
exact one-sided jump correction (zero parameters) and learned own-cell
readouts, a typed channel that tells the decoder a query is the boundary
at its own panel. A 2×2 factorial at the flagship configuration, one
node, 500 epochs, 3 seeds per arm, toggles the two independently.

| jump correction | own-cell readouts | finals (3 seeds) | mean |
|---|---|---|---|
| – | – | 0.0525 / 0.0524 / 0.0604 | 0.0551 |
| ✓ | – | 0.0148 / 0.0153 / 0.0161 | 0.0154 |
| – | ✓ | 0.0149 / 0.0151 / 0.0162 | 0.0154 |
| ✓ | ✓ | 0.0138 / 0.0140 / 0.0156 | 0.0145 |

: The trace factorial at flagship capacity, validation relative MSE.
Not reproducible from `results/`; transcribed from
`output/drivaer_trace_factorial` run logs. {#tbl-drivaerml-trace-factorial}

**The trace formulation is worth 3.8x at flagship capacity** (1.95x in
relative L2), up from 2.03x at the small reference configuration: its
effect grows with capacity, the mirror image of the kernel dictionary
below, whose effect shrinks to noise at the same configuration. Effect
sizes belong to an operating point, and the only valid attribution
measures each mechanism at the configuration actually used. The two
sub-mechanisms are near-perfect substitutes: either alone recovers about
96% of the log-gap and they finish within 0.1% of each other; enabling
both adds a final 6%. The reading consistent with the data is that the
essential content is boundary self-identification, delivered by either
channel; the factorial establishes the marginal value of a trace channel
under this protocol, not that one semantic mechanism is the carrier.
The default keeps both, and the exact correction is the principled
zero-parameter choice for any variant.

### The exact singular dictionary contributes 0–8% {#sec-drivaerml-factorial}

The factorial that varies only the kernel member dictionary at the
flagship configuration (same protocol, 3 seeds per arm) answers whether
the exact boundary-integral structure carries the DrivAerML result.

| member dictionary | finals (3 seeds) | mean |
|---|---|---|
| 2 exact + 8 learned (flagship) | 0.0138 / 0.0140 / 0.0156 | 0.0145 |
| 2 exact only (0 member parameters) | 0.0144 / 0.0138 / 0.0156 | 0.0146 |
| 8 learned only, no exact | 0.0153 / 0.0151 / 0.0167 | 0.0157 |

: The kernel-dictionary factorial at flagship capacity, validation
relative MSE. Not reproducible from `results/`; transcribed from
`output/drivaer_kernel_factorial` run logs. {#tbl-drivaerml-kernel-factorial}

Removing every exact member costs 8% (1.084x) with overlapping seed
bands; removing every learned member costs nothing (0.0146 against
0.0145). The in-distribution result is carried by the trace formulation,
typed attention and capacity, and the accurate description of the
industrial model is boundary-integral-*inspired*. Exact-kernel causation
holds where the exact kernels are the right ones (@sec-linear-suites).
What remains is precise and is the dictionary's real advantage:
**parameter efficiency**. Two closed-form, zero-parameter members beat
eight learned ones on every paired seed by about 7%, and match the full
dictionary. The same holds off-distribution: on the within-family
held-out splits below, the exact-only and learned-only checkpoints
degrade by indistinguishable ratios (1.11–1.13x against 1.11–1.14x on
wall shear), so the exact dictionary is an accuracy offset, not a
robustness slope. At the 11.4M rung, removing the learned members costs
about 9% (0.00635 against 0.00583) at one seed against a known 12% rung
spread, so the default keeps them.


### Generalization within the vehicle family {#sec-drivaerml-within-family}

Within the DrivAer family MT1 degrades by 2–3% in pressure and 7–11% in
wall shear on held-out shape-parameter extremes, and on wall shear its
degradation ratio is consistently smaller than GeoTransolver's at five
seeds per side; GeoTransolver's absolute wall-shear error is nonetheless
2.5–2.7x lower, and five paired same-sign differences cannot support a
two-sided decision at the 5% level.

The out-of-distribution protocol is defined in the dataset's own
generative coordinates: the upstream design of experiments varies 16
shape parameters, and 483 of the 484 cars carry their values. Two
held-out sets are used. The **ride-height double-extreme** takes the
top and bottom deciles of ride height (98 cars): a single-factor
extrapolation in both directions on ground-effect physics. The
**wake-topology corner** takes the joint top decile of backlight angle
and rear-end tapering (49 cars): the two-factor extreme that flips the
rear-wake topology, with a median margin along the score direction of
about 37 training-set spacings. Each model is retrained on the remaining
cars (385 and 434 respectively) with validation carved from the same
distribution, then evaluated on the full held-out set; the degradation
ratio is the held-out error divided by the same run's own
in-distribution error, so the smaller training set cancels.

Errors are evaluation-harness relative L2. Pressure is scalar; wall
shear is scored as a vector, the relative L2 of the joint components,
which exposes direction error that a magnitude-only score hides. For
both architectures the direction error is about 3x the magnitude error
(MT1 0.72 against 0.21 in-distribution; GeoTransolver 0.28 against
0.09).

| model (5 seeds each) | ride height: pressure | ride height: wall shear | wake corner: pressure | wake corner: wall shear |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MT1 flagship | 1.019–1.044 | 1.072–1.113 | 1.03 | 0.97–0.98 |
| GeoTransolver | 1.043–1.069 | 1.126–1.136 | 1.03–1.05 | 0.99 |

: Degradation ratios (held-out error over the same run's in-distribution
error, relative L2) on the two within-family held-out sets, ranges over
five seeds per architecture; both models retrained on the exclusion
splits under the same harness and protocol. Not reproducible from
`results/`; transcribed from `output/drivaer_ood` evaluation logs.
{#tbl-drivaerml-within-family}

Three facts follow. First, both models generalize well inside the
family: pressure degrades 2–7% and wall shear at most 14%, on real
aerodynamic regime shifts (wake topology, ground effect) that are
nonetheless parameter-space extrapolation within one vehicle family, not
new topologies; the wake corner does not stress wall-shear direction at
all. Second, on ride-height wall shear the five-seed ranges are disjoint
(MT1 at most 1.113, GeoTransolver at least 1.126) and GeoTransolver's
mean excess degradation is 1.4x MT1's (0.131 against 0.092); the
ordering is consistent, but with five same-sign paired differences the
minimum two-sided exact sign-test p is 0.0625, so the paired sample is
too small for a 5% decision. On pressure the ranges touch (1.044 against
1.043) and the means order the same way (1.031 against 1.056) without
seed separation. Third, the differential is in ratios only: in absolute
terms GeoTransolver's in-distribution errors are 0.061 (pressure) and
0.280 (wall shear) against the flagship's 0.167–0.180 and 0.705–0.737, a
2.5–2.7x advantage that persists on every held-out set. A zero-shot
version of the test, on the 10 and 4 held-out cars the standard training
split does not already contain, shows the two architectures degrading
alike (vector wall shear 1.12–1.13x and 1.12–1.16x).

### Cross-family transfer: every checkpoint diverges {#sec-drivaerml-crossfamily}

Evaluated zero-shot on SHIFT-SUV, a different vehicle family, through
the identical frozen inference pipeline on a 20-case pilot, every MT1
checkpoint leaves the physical range while GeoTransolver stays
structured. The prediction under test was that a model built from
boundary-integral structure transfers at least as well as a
coordinate-based one; it is refuted at every capacity and seed tested.

```{python}
#| label: fig-mt1-crossfamily

```

GeoTransolver's pressure error rises from 0.061 in-family to 0.677 on
SHIFT-SUV, an 11x degradation to roughly mean-predictor level, but the
output stays finite and structured. The three MT1 flagship seeds reach
8 × 10⁴, 4 × 10¹³ and 1.3 × 10¹⁵ and the 11.4M rung returns NaN, from
checkpoints whose own-family errors (0.107–0.180) confirm they are
healthy. Reference-length equality and sign conventions were verified
across the two datasets, so this is not a pipeline artifact. The texture
of the failure, spanning ten orders of magnitude across seeds, is an
internal magnitude blow-up rather than a wrong-answer regime.

#### The gauge changes the magnitude, not the outcome {#sec-drivaerml-transferv2}

The one number in the industrial pipeline that is neither learned nor
derived is the declared reference length, fixed at 8.0 for every
DrivAerML case. On one checkpoint, raising it to 16 and 48 brings the
SHIFT-SUV error to 5.12 and 1.71 (@fig-mt1-crossfamily, right), which
identifies the gauge as a factor in the magnitude. It is not the cause.
Six checkpoints retrained under the architecture's intrinsic gauge (a
per-sample reference length proportional to the measure-weighted RMS
boundary radius, calibrated once on the training split so that
DrivAerML's mean gauge stays at 8.0; @sec-intrinsic-gauge) were
evaluated zero-shot on the same pilot:

| checkpoint | SHIFT-SUV pressure relative L2 |
|---|---|
| GeoTransolver anchor | 0.677 |
| intrinsic-gauge MT1, seeds 42 / 43 / 45 / 46 | 5.97 × 10³ / 2.12 × 10¹⁰ / 1.90 × 10¹³ / 1.24 × 10⁷ |
| intrinsic-gauge MT1, seed 44 (in-family error 2.3x the others) | 18.2 |
| intrinsic-gauge MT1, seed 44 at half the learning rate | 2.33 × 10³ |

: Zero-shot SHIFT-SUV transfer of intrinsic-gauge retrains. The pilot
cases also served as the development set for the reference-length scan
above, so these are observations on a reused development set, not a
sealed confirmation; the orders of magnitude involved make that
distinction immaterial to the conclusion. Not reproducible from
`results/`; transcribed from `output/drivaer_transfer_v2` evaluation logs.
{#tbl-drivaerml-transferv2}

Every retrained checkpoint is finite (the fixed-gauge rung was not) and
every one is three to thirteen orders of magnitude past the
mean-predictor level. Two further observations belong here. The
intrinsic gauge introduces a seed-dependent training instability the
fixed gauge does not have (seed 44 converges to 0.0354 against
0.0139–0.0145 for its siblings, where the fixed-gauge seeds are
0.0138–0.0156). And the worst in-family seed is the best transferrer by
two orders of magnitude, while its lower-learning-rate variant, which
trains closer to the healthy band, transfers worse: at six checkpoints
spanning thirteen orders this is an observation, not a claim, but it
means in-family fit and cross-family robustness may be in tension for
this architecture. Matching the source-measure magnitude between the
families does not recover transfer either.^[No `results/` artifact; the notebook
record is @sec-nb-measmech-verdict.]

Three independent probes, sampling density (next section), measure
magnitude and geometry family, support one description: **the trained
model is a regressor fitted to a narrow operating point, and the
exact-kernel structure does not protect it outside that point.** That is
consistent with the dictionary factorial: structure that is not essential
in-distribution should not be expected to carry generalization.

### The model is a coverage-specific regressor {#sec-drivaerml-coverage}

One unchanged flagship checkpoint, evaluated on its in-distribution
reference split with nothing varied but the number of surface cells
sampled per case, has a sharp error minimum at the resolution it was
trained at and degrades in both directions, catastrophically above it.

```{python}
#| label: fig-mt1-coverage
#| fig-cap: >
#|   In-distribution pressure relative L2 of one unchanged flagship
#|   checkpoint as a function of the number of surface cells sampled per
#|   case (sources and trace queries change together). The minimum sits
#|   at the training resolution of 10,000 cells (dashed); doubling the
#|   cells costs 2.5x and quadrupling them destroys the output (24,811).
#|   How to read it: this is a property of the trained weights of this
#|   checkpoint under this sampler, not a statement about the operator at
#|   random initialisation, whose output varies about 9% under the same
#|   kind of resampling; it also does not separate the source-count and
#|   query-count effects, which move together here. Not reproducible from
#|   results/; the five values are transcribed from the resolution-sweep
#|   evaluation logs (notebook record @sec-nb-hcc-summary).

    ax.annotate(txt, (r, e), textcoords="offset points", xytext=off, ha=ha, fontsize=8.5,

ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
```

At 2,500 and 5,000 cells the error is 0.897 and 0.800 (5.4x and 4.8x the
trained value of 0.167); at 20,000 it is 0.411 (2.5x); at 40,000 it is
24,811. An operator that approximated a boundary integral would improve
monotonically with more sources. The pathology lives in the learned
weights rather than in the architecture's quadrature: at random
initialisation the operator's output varies by about 9% under
subsampling to 1.6% coverage and converges, while the trained model is
148,000x wrong at four times its training resolution. Rescaling the
measure back to its training value at the changed resolution does not
rescue it, and changing the gauge alone at fixed resolution costs 8x.

Every DrivAerML accuracy in this chapter is therefore a measurement at
one sampling density, internally comparable because every arm shares the
protocol, and not evidence about the model at any other density;
full-resolution inference (17.7 million query cells) fails for the same
reason, one step further along this curve.

### Decode cost: the checkpointed decode and the step repricing {#sec-scale-ckpt}

The kernel decoder evaluates every source-query pair, so its activation
memory scales with the product of boundary cells and queries; this, not
parameter count, is what makes MT1 an order of magnitude more expensive
than GeoTransolver to train at 10,000 cells. Checkpointing the decode in
query chunks removes the query factor from peak memory at the cost of
recomputation. The paired measurement below (one 82k-parameter
configuration, fp32, one forward-and-backward step on a 198 GB GB200,
identical per-point samples) shows what the exchange buys.

```{python}
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
import json
from pathlib import Path
from IPython.display import Markdown, display

d = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "scale_checkpoint_paired_2026-07-05.json"))
def rows(arm):
    out = {}
    for g in d[arm]["cost"]["grid"]:
        key = (g["n_boundary_cells"], g["n_query"])
        if g["status"] != "ok":
            out[key] = ("OOM", "OOM")
        else:
            out[key] = (f'{g["train_peak_bytes"] / 2**30:.1f}', f'{g["forward_backward_ms"]["median_ms"] / 1000:.2f}')
    return out
dense, ckpt = rows("dense"), rows("checkpointed")
lines = ["| boundary cells | queries | dense: peak GB | dense: step s | checkpointed: peak GB | checkpointed: step s |",
         "|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|"]
for key in sorted(dense):
    lines.append(f"| {key[0]:,} | {key[1]:,} | {dense[key][0]} | {dense[key][1]} | {ckpt[key][0]} | {ckpt[key][1]} |")
caption = (": Peak training memory [GB] and forward-plus-backward step time [s] for the dense and "
           "query-chunk-checkpointed decode on the same configuration, by boundary cells and queries. "
           "\"OOM\" is an out-of-memory failure on a 198 GB device. Step times predate the decode "
           "reimplementation described below, which makes each of them 7-14x smaller; the memory "
           "figures are unaffected by it. Data: results/scale_checkpoint_paired_2026-07-05.json. "
           "{#tbl-mt1-scale-ckpt}")
display(Markdown("\n".join(lines) + "\n\n" + caption))
```

Checkpointed, peak memory is set by the boundary count alone (4.3–8.0 GB
across a hundredfold change in queries at 5,120 cells) and the dense
decode's three out-of-memory corners all fit; the price is about 1.9x
step time at small sizes. Where the whole batched decode fits, the
checkpointing is unnecessary and costs about 10x wall-clock on 278 GB
devices; a same-seed control shows it is accuracy-neutral (×2-width rung,
seed 42: 0.0093 chunked against 0.00896 unchunked, inside the rung's
12% seed spread), so unchunked is the default wherever it fits.

The step time itself is repriced by a reimplementation of the decode
path: the closed-form kernels' einsum, which lowered to a 4.2 × 10⁷-batch
matrix multiply (a 102k-launch dispatch storm), becomes a
multiply-and-sum, and the learned members move from a sequential bitwise
loop to GEMMs with a measured tolerance (2.8–3.6 × 10⁻⁷ relative at fp32;
the closed forms stay bitwise). The two-member configuration's step
speeds up 7.2x (8.34 s to 1.16 s on a 20,480-cell trace) and the
eight-member configuration's 14.2x (43.8 s to 3.10 s). The 12.8-hour
and 14-hour training times above predate the change and are upper bounds
on the current cost by roughly an order of magnitude; the memory figures
are unchanged.

## What these results mean for the architecture choice {#sec-industrial-mt1-implications}

The industrial results place the exact-kernel line precisely. Its
accuracy gains on DrivAerML come from a boundary self-identification
channel and from capacity, both of which any architecture can have, and
not from the exact singular kernels; on separated three-dimensional
aerodynamics the potential-flow prior those kernels encode is not a
usable prior at all (the potential-flow oracle scores a relative L2 of
4.8 against 0.77 for predicting each case's mean; @sec-interior), and
on the boundary-to-interior task the kernel decoder finishes 8x behind
GeoTransolver. Within the training family it generalizes as well as
GeoTransolver in pressure and somewhat better in wall-shear ratio, at
2.5–2.7x the absolute error. Outside the training family it does not
generalize at all, and neither its exact structure nor its gauge
changes that; transfer across vehicle families is, for every
architecture tested in this book, a property of the diversity of the
training data rather than of the architecture (@sec-limits-transfer).

What the line keeps is what the controlled suites showed: parameter
efficiency (two zero-parameter exact members do the work of eight
learned ones, and the 0.8M-parameter flagship sits within 2.4x in
relative L2 of a 9M-parameter GeoTransolver), exact contracts
(similarity equivariance with the intrinsic gauge, declared linearity,
parity typing; @sec-mt1, @sec-kernel-decoder), and exact-label linear
problems, where the same decoder generalizes across boundary-condition
frequency content that soft-slice architectures cannot
(@sec-linear-suites). It pays with training memory and wall-clock an
order of magnitude above GeoTransolver's at matched sampling, and with
accuracy specific to one sampling density. The successor architecture,
MeshTransformer2 (@sec-mt2), keeps the contracts and the boundary-trace
lesson, replaces the kernel decoder with soft-slice routing, and is
compared with GeoTransolver under the fair-comparison protocol
(@sec-fair-comparison) in @sec-full-data and @sec-data-efficiency: 8.9M
against 9.0M parameters at matched tokens per case, with MT2's peak
training memory 9.8 GB as trained and 3.6 GB with the exact
pool-then-project rewrite, against GeoTransolver's 4.6 GB.
